extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or graduate students studying classical analysis and differential geometry (surface areas, series expansions)
extracted.subtask_description: Compute areas of surfaces of revolution, conical/cylindrical surface areas, centers of gravity of plane arcs, and study power-series (Maclaurin) expansions including convergence, differentiation/integration term-by-term, and classical examples (geometric series, log, arctan, sin, cos, binomial series, e^x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a zone of revolution (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIRE D'UNE ZONE. L'aire A engendrée par la rotation d'une méridienne AB autour de l'axe est donnée par A = 2π ∫ y ds (intégrale prise le long de AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the area A is the sum of the lateral areas of the infinitesimal conical frusta generated by the infinitesimal arc elements ds. When computing, express the meridian parametrically and evaluate the integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric computation of area of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point M on the meridian AB is given by x = φ(u), y = ψ(u) with u varying, then ds = sqrt(φ'(u)^2 + ψ'(u)^2) du and A = 2π ∫ ψ(u) sqrt(φ'(u)^2 + ψ'(u)^2) du.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a parameter so that M describes AB; substitute expressions for x and y and their derivatives into ds and integrate over the parameter interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation (area as sum of frusta)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula A = 2π ∫ y ds means the area is the limit of sums of lateral areas of frusta of cones generated by infinitesimal arcs; each element contributes MM' times the half-sum of circumferences of the frusta bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this viewpoint to justify the integral expression and to handle limiting/splitting arguments (useful when approximating or proving the formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a paraboloid zone (use of y as independent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabola x^2 = 2p y (axis Oy) rotated about Ox, with y as independent variable one has ds = sqrt(1 + (dx/dy)^2) dy and A = 2π ∫ y ds (written in y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace dx, ds in terms of dy to reduce to a single-variable integral; evaluate indefinite integrals as shown in the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of ellipsoid of revolution (elongated and flattened cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas are given for the area of a half-ellipsoid of revolution (both prolate and oblate) obtained by rotating an elliptic meridian x = a cos u, y = b sin u; the area reduces to 2π a^2 when b → a (hemisphere case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parametrize the ellipse, compute ds, substitute into A = 2π ∫ y ds, and often use a substitution involving eccentricity e to evaluate the integral; check limiting cases (b→a) to verify hemisphere area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a torus (Guldin special case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a circle of radius R whose center is at distance a from the axis, rotated about the axis, the torus area equals the length of the generating curve (2πR) multiplied by the circumference described by the centre (2πa): A = (2πR)(2πa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as a special case of Guldin's theorem: area = length × (2π × centroid distance). Compute by parametrizing the generating circle and integrating A = 2π ∫ y ds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling meridian crossing the axis (signs and splitting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the meridian AB crosses the axis at E, evaluate separately the areas generated by arcs on each side: A = A1 - A2 where A1 = 2π ∫_{EB} y ds (y positive) and A2 = 2π ∫_{AE} |y| ds (y negative gives negative contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split the integral along the crossing point(s) and treat the sign of y explicitly — the single integral 2π ∫ y ds then represents the difference of areas generated by parts lying on opposite sides of the axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinates of the centroid of an arc (center of gravity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a homogeneous plane arc AB with length M r = ∫ ds, the coordinates X and Y of the centroid G are given by My = ∫ y ds and Mx = ∫ x ds, hence X = (1/length) ∫ x ds, Y = (1/length) ∫ y ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mass element of an arc as its length element ds; use these moments formulas to compute centroid coordinates used in Guldin's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guldin's theorem (Pappus–Guldinus) for area
rubrics_metrics.description: The area generated by a plane line AB, rotated around an axis in its plane not intersecting it, equals the length of the line multiplied by the circumference described by its centroid: A = (length) × 2π × (distance of centroid to axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the centroid lies on the axis, the net area contributions from parts on either side cancel (Y=0). When the line crosses the axis, the theorem gives the difference of areas generated by parts on either side.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formula for differential area of a conical surface (triangle MOM')
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cone with vertex at the origin and directrix D parametrized by x=φ(t), y=ψ(t), z=χ(t), the differential area dS of the infinitesimal sector MOM' equals the area of triangle MOM', and projecting that triangle onto coordinate planes gives dS = sqrt( (y dz - z dy)^2 + (z dx - x dz)^2 + (x dy - y dx)^2 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute projections of the triangle on coordinate planes, combine via square root of sum of squares, then integrate dS (expressed in t) between parameter endpoints to get the conical surface area between two generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of dS under development (unfolding) of a cone
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression for dS does not change when the cone is developed into the plane; analytically one may rewrite dS in terms of r = OM, ds (arc length of the directrix) and dr to obtain a form invariant under development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the alternative expression involving r, dr and ds (derived in the text) to check computations and to reason geometrically using the developed (flattened) cone where the directrix length remains the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface area of a cylindrical portion bounded by two generators
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cylinder projecting a space curve AB onto the plane (A'B'), the elementary rectangle area is z·ds', so the total area S = ∫ z ds' = ∫ z sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) (or in parameter form S = ∫ z(t) sqrt(φ'(t)^2 + ψ'(t)^2) dt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the cylinder to a plane strip (flattening) and apply planar arc-length measures; integrate z times the projected arc-length to obtain the cylindrical surface area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series convergence symmetry theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: A power (entire) series ∑ a_n x^n, if it converges for some nonzero x = a, then it converges (indeed absolutely) for every x with |x| < |a|; hence the domain of convergence is an interval symmetric about zero: (-R, R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison with a geometric progression to show absolute convergence inside radius |a|; endpoints x = ±R require separate investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of interval (radius) of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The interval of convergence of an entire series is the symmetric interval (-a, +a) such that the series converges for all x in that interval and diverges for |x| > a; behavior at the endpoints x = ±a must be checked individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test endpoints separately (may converge at none, one, or both). Use ratio/root tests or term behavior to determine the radius a and check boundary behavior by substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term differentiation and integration of power series
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the interval of convergence, a power series may be differentiated or integrated term-by-term; the derived/primitive series have the same interval of convergence and represent f'(x) and ∫ f(x) dx respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When manipulating series within the radius, treat them like polynomials; be mindful of endpoint behavior when extending results to boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maclaurin series coefficients formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) = ∑ a_n x^n is representable as a power series about 0, then a_n = f^{(n)}(0)/n! and the Maclaurin expansion is f(x) = ∑ f^{(n)}(0) x^n / n! .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A necessary preliminary is that f possess derivatives of all orders finite in the interval; compute coefficients by evaluating derivatives at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy conditions for Maclaurin expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: For Maclaurin expansion to represent f(x) in an interval, it is necessary and sufficient that (1) all series coefficients are finite; (2) the series be convergent (in some symmetric interval); (3) the sum of the series equals f(x) (the last is hardest to verify).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify conditions (1) and (2) via calculus and convergence tests; justify (3) either by bounding the remainder term (using finite-increment/Lagrange remainder formulas) or other analytic continuation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remainder / error term from finite increments
rubrics_metrics.description: The error in approximating f(x) by the sum of the first n terms of its Maclaurin series is given by the finite-increments formula (a remainder involving a derivative at an intermediate point), which can be used to show the remainder tends to zero in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the general formula of finite increments (Taylor/Lagrange remainder) replacing a by 0 and h by x; estimate f^{(n+1)}(ξ) to bound the remainder and justify equality of series sum and f(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical specific series expansions and convergence domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard expansions given: geometric series 1/(1-x) = ∑ x^n for |x|<1; log(1±x) expansions for |x|<1; arctan x series convergent for |x|≤1 with slow convergence at 1; e^x, sin x, cos x expansions convergent for all x; binomial series (1+x)^m = ∑ C(m,k) x^k convergent for |x|<1 (with m arbitrary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to compute, approximate, or deduce identities (e.g. Euler's formula e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x by comparing series). Mindestimates: some series (arctan) converge slowly and may be impractical for numerical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification methods for identified series (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification approaches shown: derive differential equations satisfied by partial sums or candidate sums and match initial conditions (used to verify (1+x)^m, sin, cos expansions); use Euler's formula to relate series of e^x, sin x, cos x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct summation is unclear, differentiate/integrate the candidate sum, use functional equations, or compare derivatives at 0 to establish equality with the intended function.
